sections.html:
It records and preserves documents that touch real estate in Summit County. The Recorder Division sits inside the Fiscal Office, so the same elected Fiscal Officer who bills property tax also oversees recording. In a sale, the legal description check, the conveyance statement and the recording all run through that one county office. Deeds, mortgages and liens make up the core, and the division also keeps partnership papers, zoning amendments, military discharges, living wills and medical powers of attorney.

Anyone may view the records, with military discharges the one exception. Online search covers documents from 1988 forward, and an Index Book Archive Viewer reaches records from 1840 to 1988. The division performs no title or property searches, which leaves that task to the buyer's title company. Staff post a turnaround of three to five working days.

The county's Ohio Building in Akron is under renovation and Fiscal Office divisions are in temporary quarters. Write recorder@summitoh.net or phone before you deliver paper to a counter.

A deed passes through the Fiscal Office's transfer desk first and the recording desk second. The usual sequence:

  1. The grantor signs, and the signing is acknowledged before a notary or another listed official under R.C. 5301.01.
  2. Bring the deed and the conveyance fee statement, DTE Form 100, or the exemption statement, DTE Form 100 (EX), to the Property Transfer Department. It approves the legal description and the conveyance.
  3. Deliver by 3:30 in the afternoon if you want the transfer completed on the same business day.
  4. Take the approved deed to the Recorder Division, with recording fees on their own check.

The recording guide wants legible pages, typed names under every signature, the complete legal description on first recordings, citations to earlier recorded documents, a return address with a phone number, numbered exhibits and a stamped return envelope.

Several e-recording vendors work with the office: Simplifile, Corporation Service Company and eRecording Partners Network. Title companies commonly file that way.

Summit County recording and transfer fees
ChargeAmount
Standard recording$34.00 up to two pages, then $8.00 for each page beyond
Non-compliant filing$20.00 each
Cross-reference entry$4.00 apiece
Conveyance fee$4.00 per $1,000 of price, with the price stepped up to the next $100
Lot fee50 cents for every lot named in the description, on exempt and non-exempt transfers alike
Certified copy$1.00 added per document

The base schedule is in R.C. 317.32. The statute splits the first two pages into a $17 base fee and a $17 housing trust fee, adds $4 and $4 for every later page, and allows a county to tack on a preservation surcharge of as much as $5. Confirm the exact total with the Recording Division before you write the check.

A mailed copy of a deed costs $4, with $1 more to certify it. Walk-in copies are $2 per page. Military discharges go on record free.

The seller pays it. R.C. 319.202 has the grantee submit a value statement while the grantor covers the fee. For a sale, value means the full consideration paid or to be paid, mortgage balances and vendor's liens included. Gifts are measured by estimated open-market price, and knowingly misstating value is prohibited.

Ohio also lets counties adopt a real property transfer tax of up to 30 cents per $100 under R.C. 322.02. Summit lists the conveyance fee and the lot fee. Ask the Property Transfer Department whether any further charge reaches your deed.

A rental house carries one extra step: the auditor's endorsement tells the buyer to file rental information under R.C. 5323.02.

sections.h2: Liens and releases on a record
sections.html:
Mortgages and liens that bear on title are filed with this division, which means a title search can surface them. The fee schedule sets prices for several types:

  • IRS lien: $5.00. IRS release: $3.00.
  • Workers' compensation lien and its release: no fee.
  • Unemployment lien: no fee. Its release: $4.00.
  • Plats: $0.05 per square inch, with sizes running from $40.00 for 11 by 17 inches to $86.40 for 24 by 36 inches.
  • Township zoning regulations: $50.00. Township zoning amendments: $20.00.

Uniform Commercial Code filings carry their own fees. Call 330-643-8143 for those.

Ask your title company for the recording reference of anything it finds. The recording guide asks submitters to cite earlier documents by number, by book and page, or by recording date.

sections.h2: How a recorded deed connects to the tax bill
sections.html:
The deed decides whose name lands on the next bill, and the county handles both jobs in one office. Details that matter around closing:

  • Bills show the legal owner's name, and a bill covers the prior year because Ohio collects real estate tax one year in arrears.
  • A change to the mailing address on a tax bill must come in writing from the taxpayer to the Fiscal Officer. Recording a deed does not replace that request.
  • The owner-occupancy reduction ends when the property transfers, so a buyer who will live there applies on their own.
  • The conveyance statement asks the seller whether the home currently receives a homestead or owner-occupancy reduction.

Have the title company check the tax balance with the Treasurer division ahead of recording, so any open amount gets paid at closing. A tax certificate lien sale is avoided by paying in full or entering a payment plan with the Delinquent Tax Department.

sections.h2: Fixing a name or getting a copy
sections.html:
A recorded deed cannot be edited. To change a name, a new deed must be prepared and recorded, and only the person asking for the change or an attorney may prepare it. The new deed then goes back through the Property Transfer Department for the legal description and transfer before recording.

If you cannot find your own deed, request a copy by mail. Birth and death certificates are not kept here. Summit County Public Health issues them.

A family selling an inherited house often finds an old name or a missing transfer in the chain of title. Raise it with the title company at the start, because correcting it means a new recorded deed and another pass through the transfer desk, which adds days to a closing. Build in extra time for that, and do not schedule a closing date until the fix is on record.

Before you hand anything over, run through a short checklist. Is the deed signed and acknowledged? Do the typed names match the signatures? Is the legal description complete? Are the DTE form, the transfer fees and the recording fee on separate checks as the offices ask? Does the return address carry a phone number? A deed that fails any of these can be marked non-compliant, and the extra $20.00 charge applies on top of the normal fee.

faqs.q: How long does recording take in Summit County?
faqs.a: The Recorder Division posts three to five working days. The Property Transfer Department can finish the transfer step the same business day when forms arrive by 3:30 p.m.

faqs.q: Is e-recording offered for Summit County deeds?
faqs.a: Yes. The Fiscal Office works with Simplifile, Corporation Service Company and eRecording Partners Network, and title companies commonly file that way.

faqs.q: Will the Recorder run a title search for me?
faqs.a: No. The division performs no title or property searches. Your title company or attorney handles that.

faqs.q: Who can prepare a replacement deed to change a name?
faqs.a: Only the person requesting the change or an attorney. The new deed is recorded after the Property Transfer Department approves it.

faqs.q: Which Summit County records cannot be viewed online?
faqs.a: Military discharges. Recorded documents from 1988 forward show on the website, and older index books from 1840 to 1988 open in the archive viewer.
